extracted.intended_audience: philosophers, scientists, and theorists concerned with principles of evidence and the evaluation of human testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Outlines a reconstructed framework for evaluating human testimony in scientific matters, emphasizing reliance on experts, tests of expertness, and the scientific method as the proper spirit and means of reforming principles of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert-only testimony requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The corner-stone of the reconstructed edifice of the principles of evidence must be the recognition of the necessity of the testimony only of experts in all matters of science, and consequent absolute rejection of all testimony of non-experts, without reference to their number or the unanimity of their testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the central reform: only experts' testimony should be admitted in scientific matters. The text frames this as a radical but constructive revision, not total skepticism; definitions and tests of expertness are given to operationalize this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of science
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as the baseline for deciding what kinds of testimony require expert evaluation; implies that testimony relevant to 'science' demands methods and standards appropriate to systematized knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of expert
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert is one who can see all sides of a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the working criterion for who may be trusted as an authority; further elaborated by tests of expertness and by noting that expertness has degrees and that reputation is primarily conferred by other experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of non-expert
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-expert is one who sees but one or a few sides of a subject that has many sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms the negative side of the expert-only rule: testimony from such persons is to be absolutely rejected in matters of science, regardless of numbers or unanimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of expertness — distrust of the senses
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of the tests by which scientific expertness is judged — i.e., an expert should recognize sensory fallibility and not rely uncritically on raw sense-perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of expertness — relation of induction to deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The recognition of the relation of induction to deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert must understand how inductive and deductive reasoning interrelate in scientific inference; this conceptual grasp is a marker of expertness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of expertness — avoidance of sources of error
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoidance of all sources of error, in observation, experiment, or reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts are expected to actively seek and avoid errors in empirical and inferential work; diligence in eliminating error sources is a criterion for trusted testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of expertness — appreciation of relative importance of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The appreciation of the relative importance and non-importance of real or supposed facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts should be able to prioritize which facts matter for a question and which are irrelevant or misleading; this discriminating judgment is part of expertness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of expertness — distinguish reality and semblance
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to distinguish reality and its semblance, especially between the subjective and the objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert must be able to tell genuine objective phenomena from appearances or subjective impressions; this distinction is essential to reliable testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of expertness — maintenance of mental equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: The maintenance of mental equilibrium during experimental researches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts should preserve calm, balanced judgment under the pressures of experimentation and inquiry; emotional or unstable responses undermine expertness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method and scientific sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific method is that method of obtaining and organizing knowledge which consists in defining, so far as is possible to expert human faculties, the boundaries between the possible and the probable, between the known and the unknown. The scientific sense is the power of seeking truth through the intellect alone, uninfluenced by the emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruction of evidence principles must proceed under the scientific method and cultivated 'scientific sense'; this prescribes disciplined intellectual work, defining boundaries (possible/probable/known/unknown) and avoiding emotional bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform spirit: reconstruction not rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand is not for the rejection but for the reconstruction of human testimony; the spirit with which this should be undertaken is not skeptical, but scientific. This reform is radical and revolutionary, but discriminating and constructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides the attitude toward changing principles of evidence: aim to rebuild standards using scientific method rather than to deny possibility of knowledge or simply to be skeptical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of expertness and evaluation of pioneers
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertness has its various degrees; the highest experts are the originators, the explorers, the pioneers, the founders, the creators of science; the lowest experts are the followers... The reputation of an expert is acquired primarily through other experts, and secondarily through the judgment of mankind. The highest experts must stand at first alone and must create the standard by which they are to be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating testimony, consider the degree and type of expertness: pioneering contributions may precede broad peer recognition and still merit trust; reputation is principally a matter of expert peer evaluation rather than popular acclaim.
